newsitem.title: GERMANY: German opposition chief sees EMU crucial for jobs.
newsitem.headline: German opposition chief sees EMU crucial for jobs.

text.p: German opposition leader Oskar Lafontaine on Saturday called for a rapid introduction of a single currency as a means of easing Europe's acute unemployment problem.

Addressing a regional meeting of his Social Democrat (SPD) party in Dortmund, Lafontaine said the European Union's current system of flexible exchange rates was largely responsible for the region's 18 million jobless total.
European economic and monetary union (EMU), due to start on January 1 1999, would be the first step to end the "chaos on the financial markets".

Lafontaine's comments come after a turbulent week for Europe's architects of monetary union as the new Socialist government in France objected to details of a stability pact to ensure fiscal discipline after monetary union.
The French argue that any pact on monetary union ought to make a special case of spending for job creation.
Germany, which began the idea of a stability pact, is hoping to have the original agreement ratified at the EU summit meeting in Amsterdam next week.

Lafontaine cautioned that currency union should be accompanied by a unified taxation system and co-ordinated economic and monetary policies "which would not be made in Frankfurt," in a reference to Germany's powerful and fiercely independent Bundesbank.

Meanwhile Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber, a well-known euro-sceptic, told the Bild am Sonntag newspaper that the monetary union project should be postponed if countries failed to meet the criteria set down in the Maastricht Treaty.

"EMU will begin on January 1 1999 as a stable union or it must be postponed -- and until such a time as the preconditions are in place," he told the mass circulation newspaper, in an interview which was released ahead of publication.
Stoiber said it would be a fateful question for politicians as well as the public whether the euro would prove itself stable or not.
